title: Devanagari
hook: half of Nani's line, copied out, holds the whole week
tomorrow: why is there a stick in the middle of Nani's line?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devanagari and a guide: study and teaching together, and a traveler in Acts asking how can I, except some man should guide me. Today, the week comes back.

A card on a desk, and half of one line written inside it in careful ink: karmany evadhikaras te, ma phaleshu kadachana. In paraphrase: your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits. It took a week. And nearly every mark the week taught is somewhere in those few words.
screen: `HALF A LINE IN A CARD.` → `YOUR RIGHT IS TO THE ACTION.` → `THE WEEK IS IN IT.`

segments.voice: Walk along it. Karma opens with a conjunct, the r riding on top of the ma like a curl. Adhi carries the short i, drawn in front of the dha and said after it. Ma stands with the long a's upright stroke at its side. Phaleshu wears an e on top and a u hanging below. And no virama anywhere: every consonant that isn't joined to another keeps its a. The line was in Nani's book and on her lips long before it was in this card. That's the other half of the week: a guide. The letters let someone copy the line. Asking Nani what it means let her understand it. So here's the week in one sentence. Devanagari is a script of syllables: each consonant carries an a, signs dress it in other vowels, a stroke can stop it, and letters with nothing between them hold on. Learn those few moves and a line someone loves opens.
screen: `KARMA: A CONJUNCT.` · `ADHI: THE SHORT I IN FRONT.` · `PHALESHU: E ON TOP, U BELOW.` · `A SCRIPT OF SYLLABLES.`

segments.voice: Say the half line aloud, slowly, one piece per breath out: karmany, evadhikaras te, ma phaleshu, kadachana. Don't worry about getting it perfect. On the last breath, let it go and sit in the quiet after, with whatever action is next for you, and none of its fruit.
Devanagari, once more: the short i in front, the virama, the vowel signs, the conjuncts, all in one script, and a week of them in half a line.
For the road: Devanagari, a few small moves that open a line someone loves. A week of letters, done.

howItsDone: Students often learn a Gita verse by copying it out by hand and reciting it with a teacher, half a line at a time, until it can be said from memory.

notes: Review shape: recall holds six of the week's words (the short i, virama, phaleshu, conjunct, abhyasa, svadhyaya). Teaches Devanagari lightly as a system. Answers 1434's question.

Gita 2.47's first half is given in transliteration and paraphrased ('your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits'); no translation quoted. Check the claim that it has no virama in standard Devanagari printings (कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन): it has none; confirm.
'Adhi' here is the syllables a-dhi of adhikara (धि). 'The line was in Nani's book and on her lips long before it was in this card' refers to Priya's storyline.
